pron_note: Also heard with a hard "g": in-TRAN-si-guhnt.
means:
Refusing absolutely to compromise, negotiate, or shift position.

This isn't ordinary stubbornness about anything at all — it's specifically a **refusal to move toward the other side**. It lives in the language of talks: unions and management, coalition partners, ceasefire negotiators. *Stubborn* is personal and can even be affectionate; *intransigent* is formal, cold, and almost always an accusation — the label you pin on the party who won't deal. Note too that it describes a **stance**, not a temperament: a normally flexible person can be intransigent on one issue.
trick_unpack: The *trans* sitting in the middle is the giveaway — an intransigent party won't cross over to meet you, so no deal gets transacted.
sentences: The talks collapsed after three days, each delegation blaming the **intransigence** of the other.
He's fine about everything else, but he's **intransigent** on the dog sleeping in the bed.
etymology:
Latin **transigere** = *"to drive through to a settlement"* — *trans* (across) + *agere* (to drive, to do). Stick **in-** (not) on the front and you have someone who will not be driven across to a settlement.

That *agere* is a GRE workhorse: **transact**, **agent**, **agenda**, **agile**, **exigent**, **ambiguous** (literally "driving both ways").
one_line: Refusing utterly to compromise or negotiate.
root: agere, actum (to drive, to do) — via transigere (to settle)
